findings.where: "Where we're starting" section heading, desktop and phone (worst on desktop, where it fills the bottom third of the first screen and runs onto two lines)
findings.fault: The section heading is the biggest thing on the page. It is about twice the size of the hero's MantaHostels title and far heavier than the coral launch-news button. When you squint, the label over three bare place names wins the page, and the hero's message and primary action come second. The heading also cuts across the bottom of the first screen, so the screen ends on a giant fragment, "Where we're starting", rather than on the hero.
findings.who_objects: The backpacker landing for the first time. Their eye goes to a heading that says nothing about what MantaHostels is or what to do, and away from the one action the page wants. The founder would object too, because the brand sheet makes the single coral CTA the loudest object in the marketing zone.

findings.where: Hero, the first screen on desktop and phone: the eyebrow line, the MantaHostels title and the body paragraph
findings.fault: The hero's largest type is the brand name, which the nav bar already shows just above it. The line that says what this is, "The better way to find hostels in Indonesia.", is a small eyebrow, and it is vague: "better" gives no reason. The real reason to care (ranked on merit alone, book direct with the hostel or through your usual site) is in the smallest, faintest text in the hero. A five-second reader takes away a name and an unsupported "better", and not the findability claim the positioning rests on.
findings.who_objects: A backpacker comparing options on a phone between hops. They need the claim at a glance before they will give an email address. The brand rule is also broken: it wants the loud half to be a claim with plain mechanics directly beneath it, not a loud name with the claim whispered.

findings.where: Between the hero and the footer, the whole page body (only the "Where we're starting" heading and three place-name cards), and the footer line "Launching across Indonesia · piloting now in Bali"
findings.fault: The page asks for a launch-news email but answers none of the questions a stranger has before giving one. It doesn't say when the launch is, what they'll get at launch, how often they'll be emailed, or who is behind it beyond a first-name address. The page also contradicts itself on status. The hero says "We're building", the footer says "piloting now in Bali" (which suggests something live they can't find here), and the destination list includes Lombok although the footer names only Bali. No copyright year or date shows that the page is current.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor deciding whether to email an unknown address. With no launch timing, no idea what the emails will contain, and mixed signals on whether the service already runs, a cautious traveller doesn't write, and one who does may expect something usable now.

findings.where: Hero text column against the nav wordmark, the "Where we're starting" heading and the destination cards, on desktop
findings.fault: The hero copy and buttons sit in a column indented about 230 px from the left edge that the nav wordmark, the section heading and the card row all share. The page has two left edges that don't relate to each other, so the hero reads as a separate, floating block, not as the top of one page (continuity). The other Gestalt checks gave no fault: the cards group cleanly by proximity and common region; the ink wave and footer frame the sand section as figure and ground; nothing moves together, so common fate does not apply.
findings.who_objects: A desktop visitor scanning down the page. The jog in alignment makes the hero and the section below look assembled from different templates, which weakens the crafted, effortless feel the brand promises against a sterile or generic look.
